The Brown skua (Stercorarius antarcticus) is a large, predatory seabird that breeds across the Southern Ocean and Antarctic coastline. Eggs incubated under controlled conditions at an optimal temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after approximately 29 days [ab = approximately 29 days], a developmental period that is broadly consistent with the prolonged incubation durations observed in other large Stercorariidae. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of around 88 grams [Wwb = around 88 grams], a relatively substantial neonatal mass that provides the energetic foundation for the rapid growth trajectory that follows under intensive biparental care. This initial size reflects the considerable investment parents make in a single-egg clutch, a common reproductive strategy among skuas breeding in resource-limited polar environments.

Field records indicate that nestlings of this species achieve fledging at 55 days after hatching [tx = 55 days after hatching] under the prevailing thermal regime typical of the austral summer, where the average body temperature of a brooding adult is 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This period of chick development is characterized by a rapid accumulation of body mass, with the ultimate wet weight of adults reaching approximately 1900 grams [Wwi = approximately 1900 grams], although substantial individual variation exists, with reported values spanning from 1.2 to 2.18 kilograms depending on sex and seasonal condition. Such a large asymptotic body mass, combined with a relatively extended nestling phase, reflects the high energetic costs of somatic growth in a cold, stochastic environment.

The delay between gonadal maturation and the first successful breeding event, often spanning several years, is instead linked to social and ecological constraints such as intense competition for nesting space and the need to acquire extensive foraging experience.

The onset of the first brood, representing the age at which an individual successfully reproduces for the first time, typically occurs at 5 years after hatching [tR = 5 years after hatching] under the thermal conditions of active metabolism (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]). This substantial gap between potential and realized reproduction, lasting roughly 1,825 days, is a hallmark of long-lived seabirds with deferred maturity, an adaptive strategy that allows younger birds to forgo costly and often unsuccessful breeding attempts in favor of accumulating better body condition and site fidelity. By delaying their first clutch, skuas increase their likelihood of rearing a chick successfully, thereby offsetting the opportunity cost of lost early reproduction with a higher net lifetime reproductive output.
